ind126_larocque_thesis.title: Emma LaRocque, Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD dissertation, University of Manitoba, 1999), p. 34.

verification.note: Downloaded thesis; checked title/date and read p. 34. LaRocque relates her 1974 curriculum research to Defeathering the Indian and describes its pedagogical and resistance purposes. This is her 1999 retrospective account, not a full reading of the 1975 book or dissertation. Addendum 2026-10-14: Addendum 2026-10-14 (Claude, Van Kirk draft): reread at PDF p. 249 and n. 18 and at PDF p. 54 (OCR text layer; slips corrected). On p. 249 she describes 'the neo cross-cultural approach adopted by Native specialist scholars from about the 1960s-1980s era (Bailey, Jaenen, Trigger, Brown, Van Kirk)'. She grants that 'Compared to earlier racist material, this is, of course, a much improved approach to Native history', but writes that 'ethnological descriptions have a "distancing" effect' and that 'This process results in Othering the very people the researcher is trying to make understandable to his or her audience'. Note 18 cites Van Kirk's listing of fashion items metis women were 'very fond of' ('Many Tender Ties', pp. 101–103), with 'an unstated assumption that such interests are abnormal or "remarkable"'. The note on PDF p. 54 cites Saum, Ray and Freeman, and Van Kirk among fur-trade works that record Native resistance. Addendum 2026-10-27: Reread from the project's earlier lawful download (the repository was in maintenance): PDF pp. 8, 11, 21, 29, 37–38, 47, 70, 118–119, 135–136, 249. Walker's survey 'conservative and inadequate', 'Canadian historiography is not that benign' (p. 119); Trigger's foreword to Sioui 'a typical example of containment' (pp. 135–136); Adams's 'White Ideal' (p. 47); Said's 'pretended suprapolitical objectivity' applied to 'the Canadian academic community and its treatment of Aboriginal history' (p. 70). Addendum 2026-10-28: Edge review C (2026-10-28), from the project's earlier lawful download of the repository deposit: PDF pp. 12, 25–26, 40, 48, 50–52, 60–61, 67, 70–72, 102, 107–109, 190–191, 239–241 and 296 read. Postcolonial studies 'cannot' include Native Canadians as 'post-colonials' and its reader excludes Native writers (pp. 40, 50–51); Fanon and Memmi 'the classic sources' on internalization (p. 48); Mandelbaum's Plains Cree (pp. 107–108); fur-trade historians' 'double standard' and E. E. Rich (pp. 102, 109); Dickason's Myth of the Savage 'clearly anti-colonial' (pp. 190–191); Sioui's autohistory 'at times obscure' on method (pp. 240–241). Personal and family passages are not used.
